study.title: Psalm 92 Praise on the Sabbath, divine justice, and the flourishing of the righteous
study.overview: Psalm 92 is a song of worship for the Sabbath that unites gratitude, contemplation and trust. He begins by celebrating how good it is to praise the Lord, begins to admire the deep works and thoughts of God, contrasts the brief prosperity of the wicked with their destruction, and then portrays the just as a vigorous plant, rooted in the presence of God. The end of the psalm sums up his testimony: the Lord is upright, it is a safe rock, and there is no perversity in him.

outline.title: Proper praise for the Sabbath
outline.explanation: The psalmist opens by stating that it is good to praise the Lord, to announce his goodness in the morning and his faithfulness during the night. The use of instruments shows that praise is public, cheerful and intentional, not improvised or secondary.

outline.title: The works of God and the fall of the wicked
outline.explanation: The joy of the psalmist is born of the deeds of God. His works are great and his thoughts are deep, something that the fool does not realize. Though the wicked seem to blossom as grass, their end is certain; God remains Most High and judges with righteousness.

outline.title: The exaltation of the righteous and its lasting fruit
outline.explanation: The psalmist speaks of the strength that God grants to the righteous, the defeat of the enemies and the image of the righteous blossoms as palm and cedar. Even in old age, he continues to fruit, to declare that the Lord is straight, rock firm and without injustice.

study.context: The title indicates that this is a psalm for the Sabbath, and the commentators observe that he was associated with the cult on that day of rest. The notes highlight that the Sabbath was not only rest, but also time of holy work, especially praise and gratitude. It is not possible to state with certainty, only on the basis of the notes provided, who composed it or under what exact circumstances have been written.
study.theology: Psalm teaches that worship is an adequate response to the works of God. The Lord acts in history wisely, and his thoughts are too deep for the understanding of the foolish man. He distinguishes between just and ungodly: the prosperity of the wicked is transient, but the righteous is planted by God and receives lasting vitality. The image of the rock affirms stability, reliability and the absence of injustice in God. In evangelical reading, this sustains the confidence that divine justice may not be immediate in human eyes, but is real and certain, and that pious life bears because it is rooted in God, not in circumstances.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm shows that the Lord is faithful and just in distinguishing between the godly and the wicked; the wicked, like the grass, are quickly destroyed.
The Sabbath's own work is to praise God; the day of rest must also be a day of holy activity of gratitude.
The verse summarizes the righteousness of God: he is the rock of his people, and there is no injustice or wickedness in him.

questions: How does my worship practice express morning praise and recognized faithfulness also at night?
Do I evaluate the apparent prosperity of the wicked by the appearance of the moment, or in the light of the end that God reveals?
Is my life planted in the house of the Lord so that it continues to fruitieuting even in old age?
study.practice: Separate a weekly time, especially on the day of rest, to turn gratitude into prayer, song and reflection on the works of God. By observing apparent success of ungodly people, reject envy and reaffirm their confidence that God rules with righteousness. Also seek a life rooted in communion with God, cultivating habits that produce constant spiritual fruit, not only momentary enthusiasm.
study.uncertainty: Notes do not allow you to safely determine the precise authorship, date, location or historical circumstances of the psalm. It is also not possible to affirm, based on them, that the images of the palm tree, cedar, horn and oil should be read in a direct messianic way, although this reading can be done by some interpreters. Matthew Henry's commentary on authorship is only conjectural and should not be treated as a fact.
